04.q: Ava’s team uses a test set to choose among 30 rules, then reports the best rule’s score on that same set. Which change would give a cleaner estimate for the chosen rule?

options.text: Evaluate the winning rule on its training records.
options.feedback: The training outcomes influenced the fitted rule. A training score answers how closely it fits those examples.

options.text: Choose the rule on a validation set, then evaluate it once on a separate test set.
options.feedback: Choosing among 30 rules uses information about which cases are easy to fit. Saving an independent set until the choice is final keeps that information out of model selection.

options.text: Report the same best score rounded to fewer decimal places.
options.feedback: Rounding changes the appearance of the score. The test outcomes still influenced which rule was reported.

05.q: A classifier assigns probability 0.2 to passing. The student actually fails. Which probability goes inside the negative logarithm for this student’s binary cross-entropy loss?

options.text: 0.2, because the model reports a probability of passing.
options.feedback: The log-loss uses the probability assigned to the observed outcome. Here the outcome is failure.

options.text: 0, because the observed failure is encoded as class 0.
options.feedback: Zero names a class here. It is a label rather than the probability assigned to that class.

options.text: 0.8, because the observed class is failure.
options.feedback: There are two outcomes. The model assigns 1 − 0.2 = 0.8 to failure, giving loss −ln(0.8), about 0.223.

06.q: With three nearest neighbors, the closest records to a new student have labels pass, fail, fail in that order. Ordinary unweighted kNN uses a vote. What does it predict?

options.text: Fail, because two of the three neighbors vote for it.
options.feedback: Each of the three selected neighbors contributes one vote. Two votes for fail exceed one for pass.

options.text: Pass, because the closest record gets the deciding vote.
options.feedback: That would be the prediction with k = 1. The stated rule gives all three selected neighbors equal weight.

options.text: A tie, because both labels occur nearby.
options.feedback: A tie requires equal vote counts. The observed counts are one and two.

07.q: Four centered study logs lie exactly along the diagonal that runs from bottom left to top right in a reading-hours versus practice-hours plot. What does the first principal component capture?

options.text: A boundary separating students who pass from students who fail.
options.feedback: No exam labels enter PCA. This calculation uses the spread of the input logs.

options.text: A direction along that diagonal, because projecting there preserves the variation.
options.feedback: Differences between these logs occur along the diagonal. Projection onto it retains their spread. Reversing the sign of the direction changes the coordinate signs and preserves the same variance.

options.text: The direction perpendicular to the diagonal, because points are closest together there.
options.feedback: Projecting perpendicular to this line maps every centered log to zero. It loses the variation the first component seeks to preserve.

08.q: A hidden unit has z = wx + b and output max(0, z). For one input z = −2. How sensitive is the unit’s output to a tiny change in z that leaves z negative?

options.text: Its slope is −2.
options.feedback: −2 is the input to the activation at this example. A slope measures the change in output for a change in input.

options.text: Its slope is 1, since z contains a linear expression.
options.feedback: The preceding weighted sum is linear in its inputs. The activation afterward changes which inputs can affect this unit’s output.

options.text: Its slope is 0.
options.feedback: Both the original and slightly changed negative inputs produce output zero. The gradient flowing backward through this activation is therefore zero for this example.

09.q: Two light records have the same strongest rise and strongest fall. A classifier receives only those two numbers. Can it always determine which record fell first?

options.text: No. The representation discarded the times of the changes.
options.feedback: Two different event orders can produce exactly the same pair of maxima. A decision that depends on order needs evidence about position or time.

options.text: Yes. A deep enough classifier can reconstruct the order.
options.feedback: Extra layers operate on the numbers supplied to them. Identical inputs give a fixed classifier identical evidence.

options.text: Yes. The larger of the two numbers must have occurred first.
options.feedback: Magnitude measures how large a change was. It says nothing about when the change occurred.

10.q: You want embeddings to distinguish rising from falling records. Which transformation is a reasonable way to create a positive pair for that purpose?

options.text: Reverse the order of all readings.
options.feedback: Reversing a rising sequence makes it fall. Treating the two as equivalent would remove information needed for the downstream task.

options.text: Keep only the mean reading and repeat that value at every position.
options.feedback: The transformed record is constant. It no longer shows whether the original record rose or fell.

options.text: Add the same small constant to every reading, with no clipping.
options.feedback: For two readings a and b, (b + k) − (a + k) = b − a. Their signed change survives this transformation.

11.q: At position 2, a causal attention layer is allowed to use positions 1 and 2. The two allowed scores are equal. Position 3 has a much higher score but belongs to the future. What are the three weights?

options.text: One third, one third, one third.
options.feedback: The mask removes position 3 from the allowed set before normalization. Only two positions share the weight.

options.text: One half, one half, zero.
options.feedback: Equal allowed scores receive equal weights. They share a total of one, while the masked future position receives zero.

options.text: Almost zero, almost zero, almost one.
options.feedback: The raw future score would matter with unrestricted attention. A causal mask makes that position inaccessible.

12.q: A model assigns the observed first token probability 0.5 and the observed second token probability 0.25 given the first. What probability does it assign to this two-token prefix?

options.feedback: The second probability already conditions on the first token. Multiplying 0.5 × 0.25 gives 0.125 for the joint prefix.
Averaging the two probabilities describes their arithmetic mean. The prefix requires both token events to occur in order.
Adding would be appropriate for certain alternative events. This prefix contains both token events.

13.q: In a diffusion training example, you draw noise, add a known amount of it to a clean example, and keep the noise you drew. Why is that saved noise useful?

options.text: It identifies the single real example that every noisy input must have come from.
options.feedback: Several clean examples and noise draws can yield similar noisy measurements. The forward draw gives one supervised example.

options.text: It tells the generator which output a discriminator labeled fake.
options.feedback: A discriminator belongs to adversarial training. This denoising example obtains its target directly from the corruption process.

options.text: It supplies a target for a network learning to predict the added noise.
options.feedback: You know the sampled noise for this training draw. Comparing it with the network’s estimate teaches a denoising step at the specified noise level.

14.q: A move earns reward 1 now. The best estimated value of the next, nonterminal state is 4. With discount 0.5, what one-step target uses this observed transition?

options.text: 2.5, from discounting the sum of both values.
options.feedback: In the stated convention the first reward is immediate. Only the estimate for the future return receives the discount.
The target combines the observed reward with the discounted estimate of what can be earned from the next state.

options.text: 5, from adding the reward and the next value unchanged.
options.feedback: That calculation uses discount 1. With discount 0.5, the future contribution here is 2.

15.q: Among 100 displayed predictions, each gave its selected class confidence 0.8. Only 60 of those selected classes were correct. What does this particular group suggest?

options.text: Overconfidence in this group.
options.feedback: The stated confidence averaged 80%, and the observed correct fraction was 60%. The 20-percentage-point gap is evidence to investigate, especially on additional held-out examples.

options.text: Underconfidence, because more than half of the predictions were correct.
options.feedback: A majority being correct establishes accuracy above 50%. Calibration compares that accuracy to the stated 80% confidence.

options.text: Exactly 20 individual predictions must each have been wrong by 100 percentage points.
options.feedback: Calibration compares groups of predictions against observed frequencies. The difference between 80% and 60% does not assign a probability error to individual cases.

16.q: Two models will be compared on future student records. One model is evaluated on an easy cohort and the other on a harder cohort. What comparison would support a clearer conclusion?

options.text: Compare only the number of correct predictions from those two cohorts.
options.feedback: Counts also depend on cohort size and difficulty. They cannot isolate what changed when the model changed.

options.text: Select the most favorable subgroup for each model and report both scores.
options.feedback: Choosing favorable subgroups after inspection changes the question and makes the comparison hard to reproduce.

options.text: Freeze both models, then evaluate both on the same untouched records using the same prespecified metric.
options.feedback: This controls the examples and scoring rule. Reporting per-case or subgroup errors alongside the aggregate helps identify where one model improves or fails.
